INDUSTRIAL AND ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
Vol. 20, No. 4
Synthesis of Alcohols Higher than Methanol
from
Carbon Monoxide and Hydrogen1
Per K. Frolich and W. K. Lewis
Department
of
Chemical Engineering, Massachusetts Institute
op Technology, Cambridge, Mass.
IN
ADDITION to the methanol process previously de-
scribed2 several methods
have
been
suggested lately
for high-pressure synthesis of mixtures of aliphatic alco-
hols from carbon monoxide and hydrogen.
These processes
are all more
or less alike in so far as the experimental con-
ditions are concerned, the main difference lying in the type
of catalysts and the temperatures employed in carrying out
the synthesis.
While in the methanol process this one alcohol
is the main product of reaction, a variety of aliphatic alcohols,
ranging from methanol and up, result from the other processes.
Obviously, the products chiefly sought are the alcohols higher
than methanol and ethanol.
A German patent3 mentions the formation of a number
of oxygenated organic compounds, including alcohols, by
reactions at high pressure of carbon monoxide and hydrogen.
The catalysts
suggested
are
mixtures of metallic
oxides,
preferably with an addition of hydroxides of the alkali metals.
In trying to duplicate one of the samples quoted in this patent,
Fischer found that nothing but water resulted, while when
iron was added to the contact mass alcohols and other oxy-
genated compounds were
formed.
Fischer then worked out
his so-called “synthol” process using an iron-alkali catalyst.4
The complex mixture of liquid products obtained by this
method contains a considerable amount of aliphatic alcohols.
Apparently, the total amount of higher alcohols equals or
slightly exceeds the sum
of methanol and ethanol present.
Some of the patents relating to the manufacture of higher
alcohols6 specify the use of hydroxides of the alkali and alkali-
earth metals or the carbonates of the alkali metals, in con-
nection with what may be called typical methanol catalysts.
Two other patents6 claim the production of higher alcohols
employing the same type of catalysts, the effect of temperature
and rate of gas flow being particularly emphasized.
Starting with carbon monoxide and hydrogen, the free-
energy decrease is larger the higher the alcohol formed.
This
holds true whether water or carbon dioxide is liberated by
the reaction according to the general equations:

alcohols, and the problem therefore becomes one of searching
for the most suitable catalysts.
No matter what the reaction
is the volume always decreases in the ratio 3:1.
As for the
methanol reaction,2 pressure is required in order to secure
reasonable quantities of alcohol and depress side reactions.
The present paper describes experiments made with dif-
ferent types of catalysts in order to study the formation of
higher alcohols in accordance with the processes outlined
above.
Experimental Work
On account of the difference between the products of re-
action, the investigation can most suitably be divided into
two separate parts comprising experiments concerned with
(A) iron-alkali catalysts, and (B) metallic oxide catalysts.
The raw
materials were in both cases carbon monoxide and
hydrogen, and the reactions were carried out under high pres-
sure
at elevated temperature.
The apparatus
used
was
the same
as that described in the paper on the methanol
process.2
(A)
EXPERIMENTS
WITH
CATALYSTS
OF THE
IRON-ALKALI
TYPE
Preliminary experiments demonstrated that it was possible
to reproduce Fischer’s results using as the catalyst iron or
steel turnings impregnated with potassium hydroxide.
Char-
acteristic of this process is the formation of a liquid product
consisting of
an
aqueous and
an
oily layer.
As shown
by Fischer’s analyses,4 the aqueous layer contains in ad-
dition to water, lower alcohols, particularly methanol and
ethanol, acids, aldehydes, and ketones, while the oily layer
chiefly consists of higher alcohols and hydrocarbons.
From
ultimate analyses of the two layers and of the exit gas it was
possible to calculate the efficiency of the process for each run
—i. e., the amount of entering carbon monoxide converted into
the various products of reaction.
Usually 40
cc.
of catalyst were
employed with an exit
gas flow of 16 to 80 liters per hour, at standard conditions
of temperature and pressure (0° C. and 760 mm.),
corre-
sponding to space velocities within the range of 400 to 2000
cc. of gas per hour per cc. of catalyst.
A larger volume of
catalyst mass
(120 cc.)
was
occasionally used in order to
permit production of larger amounts of liquid per unit time
for the same
space velocities.
Unless otherwise stated the
pressure was 3000 pounds per square inch (204 atmospheres)
with a gas mixture consisting of approximately 25 per cent
carbon monoxide and
75 per cent hydrogen.
These values show that the tendency for the reactions to
go increases with increasing molecular weight of the aliphatic

General Catalyst Study
Using a catalyst composed of cast-iron turnings impreg-
nated with potassium hydroxide (run 136A), the yield of
water-soluble products was low and only a trace of oil was
obtained at 400-416°
C.
The liquid obtained
consisted
mainly of water with traces of methanol and about 1 per cent
of aldehyde.
With 0.83 per cent carbon steel impregnated with potassium
hydroxide and alumina (run 145C) fair yields were
obtained
at 411° C.
An oily product representing 5.5 per cent of the

entering carbon monoxide and an
aqueous layer containing
water and water-soluble products, corresponding to 45 per
cent of the entering carbon monoxide, were produced.
Gas-
eous products, mainly carbon dioxide and methane, amounted
to 40.8 per cent.
In
one
run
(148D) a good methanol catalyst was
placed
in the chamber above the iron-alkali-alumina catalyst used
in the previous run.
With this arrangement the gas passed
through the methanol catalyst before reaching the iron-
alkali-alumina catalyst.
At 310° C. the carbon monoxide
converted into aqueous products
was
63.9 per cent.
No
oily products were
formed.
As the temperature increased
an oily layer appeared, and at 414° C. an 8 per cent conver-
sion to oil was obtained along with a 22 per cent conversion
into aqueous compounds.
When the 8 per cent oil was ob-
tained, however, 61.2 per cent of the entering carbon monox-
ide
was
consumed in the formation of methane, ethane,
carbon dioxide, and unsatu-
rated
hydrocarbons.
At
353° C. the operation
was
more efficient.
The oil yield
was
5.4 per cent and the
yield of water-soluble com-
pounds 39.5 per cent, while
48.4 per cent of the entering
carbon monoxide went to
gaseous products.
An intermittent run of 20
hours was made with a steel
potassium hydroxide cata-
lyst at an average tempera-
ture of 427° C. (run 149C)
in order to synthesize suffi-
cient oil for a boiling-range
determination,
Of the en-
tering carbon monoxide 11.8
per cent was
converted to
oily products, 10.1 per cent
to water-soluble compounds,
and 68 per cent to gaseous
products.
The ultimate
analysis of the oily product
of this run
showed carbon
52 per cent, hydrogen
13
per cent,
and
oxygen
35
per cent, which corresponds
approximately to
C2H60.
The boiling range
is given in
Table VII.
The low-boiling fractions
were
colorless, but
as the boiling point increased the liquid became yellow and
had a pale straw color in the 179.0-209.0° C. fraction.
The
residue was
a brown, viscous liquid.
A catalyst composed of 12 per cent chromium-steel turn-
ings impregnated with potassium hydroxide was
found to
be active at moderately low temperatures, giving fair oil
yields at 300-330° C. (run 168B).
The yield of oil from
this experiment was 13.4 per cent at 334° C.; 3.4 per cent of
the carbon moxonide was
converted into aqueous products
and 56.7 per cent to gaseous products.
Section
1 of Table IV briefly summarizes the results of the
foregoing experiments under conditions of maximum oil yield.
In all cases oil production seems
to be accompanied by a
considerable loss of carbon monoxide in side reactions.
Ap-
parently this is because the higher temperature favors the
reactions CO + 3H2
=
CH4 + H20 and 2CO + 2H2
=
C02
+
CH4.
Fischer claims that below 380° C. the reaction proceeds
at a very low rate while above 460° C. there is an increasing
tendency to deposit carbon.
Between these limits the re-
action velocity increases with rising temperatures until
a
maximum of oil is obtained which is conditioned by its equi-
librium with other constituents in the gas.
If the temperature
is lower more
alcohol and less oil are
produced; if higher,
more
oil will be formed, while the alcohol in the aqueous
liquid is diminished.
Under the conditions employed by
Fischer, the best results were
realized at 410° C., provided
the rate of gas flow was adjusted to secure
the establishment
of equilibrium.
From this it would seem that a novel result
was obtained in run
168B (Table IV), in which a compara-
tively large ratio of oil to aqueous products was obtained at
334° C. using a 12 per cent chromium steel-alkali catalyst.
A rather detailed study was
therefore made of the effect
of variations of the chromium content of the catalyst.
Variation
of Chromium
Content
of Chromium
Steel-
Potassium
Hydroxide Catalyst
A list of the various catalysts containing iron and chro-
mium is given in Table I.
In testing these catalysts
the experimental conditions
were, in general:
pressure
3000 pounds per square inch
(204
atmospheres),
tem-
perature between 300
° and
450° C., and an exit rate of
gas flow of approximately
50 liters per hour with an
entering gas containing
about 25 per cent of carbon
monoxide and 75 per cent
hydrogen, the volume of the
catalyst being 40 cc.
As
a
whole the results
were
decidedly unsatisfac-
tory.
Either no reaction or
only very slight activity was
observed in every case
ex-
cept with catalyst II—30—1
(2.75
per
cent
chromium
steel).
In section 2 of Table
IV the yields previously ob-
tained with a catalyst con-
taining
12 to
14 per cent
chromium
steel
(II-16-2)
are compared with the
re-
sults from this experiment.
The reduction of the chromium content of the steel from
12-14 per cent to 2.75 per cent, with an accompanying in-
crease
in the carbon content from 0.35 per cent to 0.9 per
cent, has not materially changed the yield of aqueous and oily
products, but it has decreased the yield of gaseous products
from 56.7 per cent to 38.5 per cent.

The
synthesis of
alcohols higher than
methanol
from carbon monoxide and hydrogen under high pres-
sure
has been studied for two distinctly different types
of catalysts—(1) iron impregnated with alkali, and (2)
mixtures
of metallic
oxides.
Particularly
the
composition
of
the
iron-alkali
catalyst has been varied within
wide limits.
In general,
the results obtained with
this type of catalyst show
that it is very difficult
to suppress side reactions leading
to the formation
of carbon dioxide, methane, water,
and elementary carbon.
The liquid product usually
separates in two
layers—one containing water
in pre-
dominating quantities, the other being of oily character
and consisting of complex mixtures
of the simpler
oxygenated aliphatic compounds as well
as hydrocar-
bons of varying boiling point.
When
operated
at
sufficiently high temperatures,
catalysts
composed
of
mixtures
of
metallic
oxides
give considerable amounts
of higher alcohols in addition
to methanol, water, and gaseous by-products.
For both types of catalysts the percentage of carbon
monoxide lost
in
undesirable
side reactions
is quite
serious, and in
this
respect the iron-alkali
catalysts
are
inferior
to the oxide mixtures.

In view of these data and the negative results with alloys
of high chromium content (Table I), it
seems that a low-
chromium steel offers the best possibilities of efficient oil
formation.
It
should be pointed out, however, that the
increase in the carbon content of the steel may also be re-
sponsible for the decrease in- the formation of gaseous prod-
ucts, since advantages are
claimed for the use of catalysts
containing carbon.8
Variation
in Potassium
Hydroxide Content
of Chromium
Steel-Potassium
Hydroxide Catalyst
In order to determine the effect of the potassium hydrox-
ide content on the activity of the chromium steel-potassium
hydroxide catalyst, three runs
were
made with catalysts of
the compositions given in Table II.
The experimental con-
ditions under which this comparison was
made were:
tem-
perature about 330° C., entering gas flow of 20 to 25 liters
per hour, and pressure 3000 pounds per square inch (204
atmospheres) with an entering gas containing 40 per cent
carbon monoxide.
The results
are
shown in section 3 of
Table IV.
PERCENT
POTASSIUM -OXIDE
IN CATALYST
The best yields were
obtained with the catalyst (11-25-
1) containing the smallest amount of potassium hydroxide
(2.2 per cent potassium oxide).
There is apparently little
difference in the aqueous and oily yield with 4.5 per cent
and 8.5 per cent potassium oxide, but a considerable change,
from 31.6 per cent to 79.4 per cent, is observed in the conver-
sion of carbon monoxide to gaseous products.
(Figure 1)

Content

a

were
made to determine the effect
of the carbon monoxide concentration in the gas on the yields
of the various products.
In section 4 of Table IV the re-
sults of these experiments
are
summarized and compared
with the yields obtained in
run
168B.
The experimental
conditions were
the same
as those outlined above, except
that the entering rate of flow was
50 to 55 liters per hour.
A catalyst containing 4.5 per cent potassium oxide (II—16—4,
Table II) was
used throughout.
These data show that the best yields are
obtained with

interest also to note that in a run
(210A) where a flow of
23.2 liters per hour was used with a gas containing 67.1 per
cent carbon monoxide, 15.8 per cent conversion to oily prod-

obtained along with 48.8 per cent conversion to
gaseous products.
However, in this experiment very heavy
carbon deposition took place in the chamber.
This obser-
vation
confirms
Fischer’s
conclusion
that
high
carbon
monoxide concentrations give increased oil yields but also
cause
carbon deposition.

A run

An iron-alkali catalyst (II—16—5, 12 to 14 per cent chromium
steel) was placed in the normal position in the middle of the

The
gases, after leaving this catalyst,
passed

The increased losses

Tests of Miscellaneous
Catalysts
A large number of catalysts of widely varying composition
and including an active ammonia catalyst of the iron-alkali
type, obtained by courtesy of the Fixed Nitrogen Laboratory,
Washington, D. C., were
also tried out.
The results, which
are
not particularly promising, may be summarized thus:
There is practically
no activity with catalysts containing
iron oxide and potassium hydroxide.
Nickel steel (10 per
cent) seems to be rather violent in its action, since particles of
carbon were
observed in the product;
no oils were
formed,
however.

Experiments with
a Methanol
Catalyst Followed by an
Iron-Alkali
Catalyst
Several experiments
were
made by first converting
a
portion of the entering gas mixtures to methanol and then
passing the methanol-carbon monoxide-hydrogen mixture
through an iron-alkali-higher alcohol catalyst.
A good meth-
anol catalyst (zinc-chromium, 1-51-1) was used and operated
at 283° and 325° C.
The entering rate of gas flow was
80
liters per hour at the lower temperature and both 20 and
80 (approximately) liters per hour at the higher tempera-
ture.
Considerable liquid was formed in all runs, but only
at 325° C. did a few drops of oily product appear.
Runs
178D and 178E were
made at 325° C., the former with an
inlet rate of 30 liters and the latter with 80 liters per hour.
The yields in both runs, based on ultimate analyses of the
products, are shown in section 5 of Table IV.
It was noticed
that the lower rate of flow produced more oil than the higher,
although the actual amounts were
small.
From the table
it is seen that this higher oil formation corresponds to a higher
percentage of entering carbon monoxide being converted to
gaseous products, while the percentage of carbon monoxide
converted to total liquid products is about the same for both
runs.
Higher alcohols
were
detected by fractionation of
both products but not identified.
Since fair
efficiencies
were
obtained with
considerably
smaller losses than shown by an iron-alkali catalyst alone,
two additional runs
of about 24 hours’ duration were
made
in order to obtain sufficient product for more
complete exami-
nation.
The experimental conditions of the two long runs
(182 and 183) were similar to those of run
178D, except that
in run
183 the period of reduction of the catalyst was
3
1/<¡
hours instead of the usual
1 3/< hours at 10 atmospheres and
150° C.
As shown in section 6 of Table IV, considerable
difference was
found between the efficiencies of conversion
in the two runs.
Only a few drops of oily product appeared
in each case.
Fractionations disclosed higher alcohols while
methanol
was
present in predominating quantities.
The
product from run
182 contained about 75 per cent methanol,
while 183 was lower in methanol (45 per cent) but contained
a larger quantity of higher alcohols.
(B)
EXPERIMENTS
WITH
METALLIC
OXIDE
CATALYSTS
Extensive
preliminary
experiments
demonstrated
that
temperature entered
as
a most important variable when
catalysts composed of metallic oxides were
employed.
Thus,
higher alcohols did not form unless temperatures around
450° to 500° C. were
reached, which is considerably higher
than the 300° to 350° C. required for methanol formation.
The following catalysts
were
made up:
1-48-1 was prepared by dissolving pure zinc oxide in molten
potassium dichromate.
The mass
was then cooled and crushed.
1-39-1 was prepared by mixing intimately 8 parts zinc oxide,
10 parts chromium trioxide, and 8 parts of barium hydroxide.
Copper was used as a supporting medium.
1-47-1
was
made from zinc oxide, ammonium dichromate,
and potassium carbonate.
After mixing, the materials were dried
in an
oven
to remove
the ammonia.
1-70-1 consisted of barium carbonate and copper hydroxide
on
a copper support.
The barium carbonate amounted to only
0.5 per cent of the total catalyst.
The results of experiments made with these catalysts are
listed in Table V.
As an example of the type of products
formed, we may consider the liquid products from runs
278A
and B, which were combined in order to obtain a large sample
for fractionation.
In determining the constituents of the
different fractions three separate
means
were
employed—

Formation

COMPARISON
OF RESULTS
WITH
TWO
TYPES
OF CATALYSTS
It is interesting to compare the best results obtained with
the two types of catalysts (Table VII).
On the basis of
entering carbon monoxide, 13.9 per cent of useful products
were obtained with the oxide catalyst, 10.5 per cent appearing
in the oily layer and 3.4 per cent in the aqueous layer.
The
yield of useful products other than methanol was
11.3 per
cent.
Of the 16.8 per cent of useful products obtained with
the iron-alkali catalyst, 13.4 per cent appeared in the oily
layer, and 3.4 per cent in the aqueous layer.
Although the
iron-alkali catalyst gives a slightly larger yield of useful prod-
ucts in the oily layer, the waste products formed by the
reaction are disproportionately higher than with the oxide
catalyst.
Another interesting point of comparison lies in the type
of product obtained by the two catalysts as shown by the
boiling ranges given in Table VII.
Although the two give
about the same amount boiling below 80° C., a marked diver-
gence occurs
above this point.
Analyses have already been
given showing that the products from the oxide catalyst
consist mainly of higher alcohols.

oily products obtained in the two most efficient experiments
with
a chromium steel-alkali catalyst are

VIII.
The exact nature of the substances obtained with
the iron-alkali catalysts has not been determined.
In view
of Fischer’s results, however, the oil is considered as
con-
sisting of a mixture of higher alcohols, aldehydes, ketones,
and acids, together with some
higher hydrocarbons.

Conclusions
From a study of these data it is apparent that the portion
of carbon monoxide lost in wasteful side reactions is con-
siderable for both iron-alkali and metallic oxide catalysts.
While a certain formation of carbon dioxide may be unavoid-
able owing to the type of reactions involved, there can
be
no doubt that the high temperature of operation is respon-
sible for a large part of the losses.
Thus, it has been noted
all through this investigation, as well as in the study of the
methanol reaction, that the higher the temperature the greater
the tendency for wasteful side reactions to occur.
This detri-
mental feature might be counteracted by the development
of more
active catalysts which would permit operation at
lower temperatures.
The side reactions would be further
suppressed by employing even higher pressures.
From the
point of view of losses, the metallic oxide catalysts
seem
most promising in that they do not possess the marked tend-

THE
alkaline solutions used for treating petroleum dis-
tillates have
been found to contain phenolic
com-
pounds which are readily detected by a strong odor
resembling
cresols
when
such
solutions
are
neutralized.
Although the phenols comprise a very small percentage of
most distillates, they may accumulate to the extent that
the disposal of waste liquors around refineries may become
no small problem.
The pollution of small streams or larger
bodies of water near city water supplies and the odors arising
from caustic wash waters, especially those used in treating
cracked distillates, are some
of the complaints with
which refiners have already
been confronted.
A solution to the problem
of a means
for disposal of
such materials is reached in
many refineries by
one
of

The writers have recently examined the oil extracted from
cracked gasoline by washing with caustic soda prior to treating
with acid, and find that this oil, precipitated from the aque-
ous alkali by dilute sulfuric acid, consists chiefly of cresols and
phenol.
Gatlin3 has published a brief description of cresylic acid sepa-
rated from caustic soda which had been used in the first stage
of a continuous unit treating cracked distillates.

It

The

of recovery and refining;

Fuel

A better use will probably be found after the

For this reason
the present investigation was
undertaken.
Previous Work
A survey of the literature disclosed that little work had
been done on the investigation of petroleum phenols.
Other
chemists have noted the presence of phenols in cracked dis-
tillates, but are not in entire agreement concerning the nature
of the compounds.
